clinicalPearls: Incomplete closure of the eyelids, leaving the ocular surface exposed and at risk of drying
The commonest cause is facial (seventh nerve) palsy weakening the orbicularis oculi
Nocturnal lagophthalmos, exposure from proptosis or lid retraction, and cicatricial lid shortening are other causes
A protective upward rotation of the globe on attempted closure (Bell phenomenon) helps guard the cornea
Exposure keratopathy, ranging from punctate staining to ulceration, is the main threat to sight
Management centres on intensive ocular surface lubrication and protection, with surgical measures for persistent cases
reference.pathophysiology: Lagophthalmos occurs when the eyelids cannot fully appose, whether from weakness of the orbicularis oculi (as in facial nerve palsy), mechanical factors such as proptosis or lid retraction, or cicatricial shortening of the lids. Failure of the normal blink and closure leaves the interpalpebral cornea and conjunctiva exposed, so the tear film evaporates and the surface dries. Without an effective Bell phenomenon or protective measures, exposure leads to epithelial breakdown, keratopathy and potential ulceration or perforation.
additionalDifferentials: Thyroid eye disease with proptosis or retraction
additionalInvestigations: Measurement of the closure gap and assessment of blink
Corneal examination with fluorescein for exposure keratopathy
Assessment of the Bell phenomenon and corneal sensation
Evaluation for facial nerve palsy or orbital cause
redFlags: Reduced corneal sensation compounding exposure risk (neurotrophic component)
Progressive or severe exposure with visual loss
reference.prognosis: With diligent lubrication and protection the cornea can be preserved, and many neurogenic cases improve as the palsy recovers; persistent or severe exposure may need surgical lid procedures to protect sight.
pitfalls: Underestimating exposure risk when corneal sensation is also reduced
Relying on infrequent lubrication in significant lagophthalmos
Overlooking nocturnal lagophthalmos as a cause of morning irritation
Failing to protect the eye during the recovery phase of facial palsy
management: Intensive ocular surface lubrication is the mainstay - frequent artificial tears through the day and a lubricating ointment at night
Provide mechanical protection with lid taping, a moisture chamber or an overnight eyelid dressing to shield the exposed cornea
Treat the underlying cause, such as managing facial nerve palsy or thyroid eye disease and addressing proptosis or lid retraction
Offer surgical measures for persistent exposure - upper-lid weight implantation, tarsorrhaphy, lower-lid tightening or correction of cicatricial lid shortening
Monitor the cornea with fluorescein for exposure keratopathy and treat secondary microbial keratitis promptly
Refer to ophthalmology or oculoplastics for assessment and surgical planning
Escalate urgently if corneal ulceration or perforation threatens sight
